title: The Passion Narrative: The Story of Jesus’ Crucifixion and Resurrection
subtitle: The Gospel accounts, the Christian confession, and the Quranic account
summary: The four Gospels agree on the central Christian claim that Jesus was crucified and that his followers believed he rose, but they arrange and describe parts of the final days differently. Christianity makes the cross the center of salvation. The Quran honors Jesus while denying that his enemies successfully killed him and directing salvation toward faith, repentance, mercy, and worship of God alone.

sections.title: The Question in Brief
sections.body: The four Gospels agree on the central Christian claim that Jesus was crucified and that his followers believed he rose, but they arrange and describe parts of the final days differently. Christianity makes the cross the center of salvation. The Quran honors Jesus while denying that his enemies successfully killed him and directing salvation toward faith, repentance, mercy, and worship of God alone.

sections.title: The Christian Story in the New Testament
sections.body:
Matthew 26–28, Mark 14–16, Luke 22–24, and John 18–20 narrate Jesus’ final days. They share a broad sequence: a final meal, arrest, trial, crucifixion under Pontius Pilate, burial, and an empty tomb. Each proclaims Jesus's resurrection. Matthew, Luke, and John narrate appearances; the earliest surviving manuscripts of Mark end at 16:8 with an announcement rather than an appearance scene. Mark's later longer ending, 16:9-20, includes appearances and is received as canonical in several Christian traditions. The [USCCB notes on Mark 16](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/16) explain that textual distinction. The accounts differ in chronology and detail, but all make the crucifixion and resurrection decisive.

Paul’s earlier summary in 1 Corinthians 15:3-8 says Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to followers. Christian theology treats this as the heart of the apostolic proclamation.

sections.title: Where the Gospel Accounts Differ
sections.body:
The Gospels are four narratives, not identical transcripts. They vary in the people emphasized at the tomb, sayings from the cross, the timing of scenes, and the order of appearances. Christian interpreters often see selective reporting and complementary perspectives. Historical-critical scholars see distinct literary purposes and sources.

The differences do not remove the shared Christian claim. Each Gospel makes Jesus’ death and the proclamation of his resurrection central. The deeper question is whether these events should be understood through the Christian or Quranic account.

sections.title: Why the Resurrection Is Central to Christianity
sections.body:
Christianity understands the crucifixion as an atoning death and the resurrection as God's vindication of Jesus. The New Testament connects them to forgiveness, reconciliation, and hope beyond death. Paul says that without the resurrection, Christian preaching and faith would be empty.

The disagreement is not over whether Christians take these events seriously. It is over whether the crucifixion occurred and whether Jesus is a divine savior.

sections.title: The Quranic Account of Jesus
sections.body:
The Quran honors Jesus as the Messiah, son of Mary, and messenger of Allah. Quran 4:157 states that his opponents did not kill or crucify him, while Quran 4:158 states that Allah raised him.

The Quran does not name another person in Jesus’ place. Classical commentators offered more than one explanation of how the event appeared to his enemies. The core Islamic belief is clear: Allah saved Jesus, raised him, and his enemies did not kill him.

sections.title: The Central Difference
sections.body:
Christianity sees the crucifixion and resurrection as the saving climax of Jesus’ divine mission. Islam sees Jesus as a human messenger whom Allah protected and rejects salvation through the death of a divine son.

This is not a minor chronological question. It concerns revelation, God's nature, Jesus' identity, and forgiveness. Each account should be considered from its primary texts.

sections.title: Why This Matters: The Passion Narrative: The Story of Jesus’ Crucifixion and Resurrection
sections.body: The four Gospels agree on the central Christian claim that Jesus was crucified and that his followers believed he rose, but they arrange and describe parts of the final days differently. Christianity makes the cross the center of salvation. The Quran honors Jesus while denying that his enemies successfully killed him and directing salvation toward faith, repentance, mercy, and worship of God alone.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
sections.body:
Q: Do the four Gospels tell one identical Passion Narrative?
A: No. They share the central story but differ in literary arrangement and individual details. Christians commonly read the accounts as complementary, while historical-critical scholars analyze the differences as evidence of each author's sources and aims.

Q: Does Islam deny Jesus?
A: No. Belief in Jesus as the Messiah and a messenger of Allah is required in Islam. The Quran affirms his virgin birth and miracles by Allah’s permission while rejecting his divinity and crucifixion.

Q: Does the Quran identify someone else who was crucified?
A: No. Quran 4:157 does not name a substitute. Muslim commentators have differed about the details, but the verse’s central claim is that Jesus was not killed or crucified by his enemies.

Q: Why does this disagreement matter?
A: The crucifixion and resurrection are central to Christian salvation theology, while Islam’s account safeguards the absolute oneness of God and Jesus’ status as His honored messenger.

sections.title: Further Reading
sections.body:
- **The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought**. Todd Lawson. A scholarly study of Muslim interpretations of Quran 4:157.
- **The Resurrection of Jesus: A New Historiographical Approach**. Michael R. Licona. A detailed Christian historical defense of the resurrection.
- **The Historical Figure of Jesus**. E. P. Sanders. A widely used introduction to historical study of Jesus and the early Christian movement.

quranVerses.arabic: وَقَوْلِهِمْ إِنَّا قَتَلْنَا ٱلْمَسِيحَ عِيسَى ٱبْنَ مَرْيَمَ رَسُولَ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ وَمَا صَلَبُوهُ وَلَٰكِن شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ ۚ وَإِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ ٱخْتَلَفُوا۟ فِيهِ لَفِى شَكٍّۢ مِّنْهُ ۚ مَا لَهُم بِهِۦ مِنْ عِلْمٍ إِلَّا ٱتِّبَاعَ ٱلظَّنِّ ۚ وَمَا قَتَلُوهُ يَقِينًۢا
quranVerses.translation: And [for] their saying, "Indeed, we have killed the Messiah, Jesus, the son of Mary, the messenger of Allah." And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him; but [another] was made to resemble him to them. And indeed, those who differ over it are in doubt about it. They have no knowledge of it except the following of assumption. And they did not kill him, for certain.

bibleVerses.text: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that he was buried, that he was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that he appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve. Then he appeared to over five hundred brothers at once, most of whom remain until now, but some have also fallen asleep. Then he appeared to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all, as to the child born at the wrong time, he appeared to me also.
